item.title: Opening the Black Box: Agentless Threat Detection for Virtual Appliances
item.description:
FortiGate devices are a prime attacker target: internet-facing, highly privileged, and invisible to traditional EDR. Wiz outlines agentless detection playbooks covering the full post-exploitation chain.
Key findings:
- 51.9% of cloud environments run at least one virtual appliance; 12% run FortiGate specifically. The 2026 FortiBleed campaign compromised credentials for roughly 75,000 devices across 194 countries. Salt Typhoon exploited CVE-2023-48788; UNC3886 used CVE-2022-41328 to deploy the CASTLETAP backdoor via FortiManager script abuse, then pivoted to VMware ESXi. A zero-day, CVE-2026-24858, was exploited to authenticate via SSO, create super_admin accounts, and delete logs.
- Post-compromise persistence follows a fast pattern: attackers authenticate via FortiCloud SSO using disposable addresses (support@openmail[.]pro, cloud-noc@mail[.]io), create a local admin (ssl-admin, backupadmin, helpdesk) with super_admin profile, MFA disabled, and trusthost=0.0.0.0/0, then immediately run "show full-configuration" to extract reversible-encrypted credentials, all within 10 minutes.
- Key log IDs to ingest: 32001/32002/32003 (auth), 44547 (object config, covers account creation, NAT/VIP, cert changes), 44548 (CLI commands executed), 32095 (config download via GUI), 32052 (FortiManager script push). For lateral movement, hunt subtype=local traffic logs for ICMP (proto=1) or unexpected outbound connections originating from the firewall itself.

item.title: Intercepting Android WebView traffic under new certificate validity requirement by Chromium
item.description:
Burp Suite's 1-year proxy cert now fails Android WebView interception silently. Chromium's cert validity enforcement (CERT_VALIDITY_TOO_LONG, net_error -213) breaks TLS interception without any app-side pinning in place.
Key findings:
- Chromium in Android WebView enforces max cert lifetimes per CA/B Forum Baseline Requirements. Certs issued on or after March 15, 2026 must be 200 days or fewer. Burp generates a 365-day cert (notAfter one year out), which now hard-fails with SSL error code 1, net_error -213 in logcat. mitmproxy generates shorter-lived certs and intercepts cleanly.
- The check lives in CertVerifyProc::HasTooLongValidity inside libwebviewchromium.so. It applies to any leaf cert marked as issued by a known root, meaning your Burp CA cert alone does not exempt the generated leaf from the validity window check.
- Three workarounds, easiest first: (1) uninstall WebView updates via adb shell dumpsys webviewupdate to revert to version 113; (2) chain mitmproxy on port 9090 as upstream proxy to Burp on port 8080 using --mode upstream with --ssl-insecure; (3) Frida-hook both cert_verify_proc at offset 0x3e015f8 and CachingCertVerifier::Verify at 0x3e00068 in libwebviewchromium.so after disabling multiprocess via adb shell cmd webviewupdate disable-multiprocess.
Before your next Android WebView assessment, confirm your proxy cert lifetime with openssl x509 -noout -dates.

item.title: Dolphin X Stealer Targets 300+ Apps and Profiles Users with AI
item.description:
Dolphin X infostealer targets 300+ apps with a server-side mutation engine and an AI Profiler that auto-ranks victims by value, exposing cloud, DevOps, and wallet credentials in a single archive.
- Discovered advertised on a cybercrime forum by alias "Kontraktnik," Dolphin X collects from 9 browsers, 100+ wallet extensions, 65 desktop wallets, 10 password managers, and 30 cloud CLI tools. On a developer machine, .env files and SSH directories often hold over-scoped, long-lived credentials reaching cloud consoles, build pipelines, and production environments.
- The build process is remote: operators configure C2, persistence, and evasion in a desktop panel, then submit to backend.thedolphinx[.]top:8443 for server-side compilation. This means the vendor touches every binary before delivery, enabling a tiered mutation engine that rewrites control flow, shuffles import tables, and rewrites PE timestamps, directly targeting hash-based blocklists and brittle YARA rules.
- The AI Profiler scores each infected host on app usage, browsing activity, and installed software, returning a ranked daily summary so operators can triage thousands of machines and focus on the highest-value targets first.
Detection should focus on behavior, not file hashes: explorer.exe running under a non-default desktop is a strong HVNC indicator regardless of packing. Keep long-lived credentials off disk and out of project directories.

item.title: AWS CloudTrail Cheat Sheet for Incident Responders | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Invictus IR releases a free AWS CloudTrail cheat sheet mapping high-value event names to MITRE ATT&CK phases, built from real incident experience and adversary simulation.
Key details:
- CloudTrail captures both management events (control plane: creating/deleting S3 buckets) and data events (data plane: reading/writing S3 objects). Both GUI and API calls are logged in JSON, and the Event name field is the primary identifier for triage.
- The cheat sheet was built from three sources: real AWS incidents investigated by Invictus IR, adversary simulation using Stratus Red Team in a test environment, and practitioner threat modeling to fill gaps. That pedigree makes it more reliable than purely theoretical lists.
- Events are organized by MITRE ATT&CK phase, letting responders map CloudTrail noise to reconnaissance, persistence, privilege escalation, exfiltration, and other stages quickly during active investigations.
- The sheet is available on GitHub in multiple formats plus a GitHub gist for easy copy-paste during live response, lowering friction when you need to build a query or detection rule fast.
Practitioner takeaway: pull the cheat sheet from the Invictus IR GitHub and load the relevant Event names into your Athena queries or SIEM rules before your next AWS engagement. Sorting your CloudTrail results against ATT&CK phases cuts triage time significantly on noisy tenants.

item.title: Azure VM Command Execution using Third-Party Extensions – Chef
item.description:
Attackers with a single Azure RBAC permission can deploy a rogue Chef extension to any VM and execute arbitrary code as root, stealing Managed Identity tokens while blending into legitimate admin activity.
Key findings:
- The only permission needed is Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write, held by Owner, Contributor, Log Analytics Contributor, Virtual Machine Contributor, and several lesser-known roles including Defender for Servers and Desktop Virtualization Contributor. On engagements, Domain Controllers frequently run as Azure VMs, making any principal with this permission effectively a Domain Admin.
- Attack chain: stand up chef-zero (no auth, no input validation) on a public IP, craft a malicious cookbook that curls the IMDS endpoint at 169.254.169.254 to steal the Managed Identity OAuth token and exfiltrates it OOB, then deploy ChefClient or LinuxChefClient extension via az vm extension set pointing bootstrap_options.chef_server_url at the rogue server.
- Host artifacts to hunt: on Linux, check /var/lib/waagent/Chef.Bootstrap.WindowsAzure.LinuxChefClient-[version]/config/0.settings for a suspicious chef_server_url and /var/log/azure/Chef.Bootstrap.WindowsAzure.LinuxChefClient/chef-client.log for executed commands. On Windows, C:\chef\0.settings and C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\Plugins\Chef.Bootstrap.WindowsAzure.ChefClient\[version]\chef-client.log hold the same evidence.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2079718654686715963

item.title: The Procurement Trap: Inside an AiTM Campaign Targeting Global Institutions
item.description:
AiTM phishing campaign hits universities, EU and UN agencies using compromised aged domains, rotating PhaaS kits, and procurement lures to steal MFA-protected sessions in real time.
Key details:
- Attack chain: phishing emails sent from compromised Outlook accounts use RFI and bid-invitation lures, directing victims through fake document portals (testserveren[.]com, barifurniture[.]net), Cloudflare Turnstile or actor-hosted CAPTCHA, then cloned Microsoft login pages impersonating targets like the European Investment Bank. Email addresses are embedded in URL paths to personalize the illusion.
- The actor rotates three PhaaS kits: EvilProxy (reverse proxy, active since 2022), FlowerStorm/Storm-1167 (likely Rockstar2FA rebrand, reverse proxy targeting M365), and Kali365 (device code abuse plus AiTM session capture, first seen April 2026). RDGA patterns distinguish the kits: FlowerStorm uses corporate-buzzword .de domains; EvilProxy uses corporate-buzzword .net/.com.
- Infrastructure fingerprint: compromised aged domains averaging 6-plus years old, injected with an index.php to serve phishing content. No ownership change indicators. RDGA domains include usersatisfactionlab[.]de and q1evaluationperformance[.]net.
- MFA is not a defense here. Session cookies and tokens are intercepted in real time as victims complete legitimate MFA flows, giving the actor an authenticated session without ever cracking a code.

item.title: Detecting Emails Sent Using Unexpected Languages (+KQL Query)
item.description:
A KQL hunting query flags emails where the detected language mismatches the sender IP's expected country language, surfacing a low-signal indicator useful for layered phishing and BEC investigations.
Key details:
- The query uses Microsoft Sentinel's EmailEvents table, resolving SenderIPv4/IPv6 with geo_info_from_ip_address(), then comparing the detected EmailLanguage (first two characters, lowercased) against a country-to-language mapping loaded via externaldata() from a GitHub-hosted CSV, keeping maintenance outside the query itself.
- Country-language mappings are stored in a semicolon-delimited CSV, split into an array at runtime. Emails where the detected language is absent from that array and not flagged as unknown ("un"/"xx") become hunting candidates, scoped to low-volume senders (EmailCount < 10) to reduce noise.
- Tuning is built in: exclude high-FP countries, allowlist trusted sender domains, and adjust volume thresholds. The author explicitly cautions this is not a standalone phishing detector, its value comes when stacked with signals like newly registered domains, SPF/DKIM failures, or unusual sender behavior.
- The artifact cluster to chase: SenderIP, Country, DetectedLanguage, SenderDomains, ThreatTypes, and Subject lines, all surfaced per sender in the output summarize.
Takeaway: Pull the KQL from the report and run it against EmailEvents in Sentinel.

item.title: Exploitarium: Inside the Archive Behind the Mass 0-Day Drop
item.description:
The "exploitarium" GitHub archive has grown to 35 project folders and 204 tracked files of uncoordinated PoC releases, with CVE-2026-55200 in libssh2 as its most critical output: a pre-auth heap out-of-bounds write reachable before credentials are checked.
- CVE-2026-55200 targets libssh2 through 1.11.1. An insufficient upper-bound check on packet_length in ssh2_transport_read() causes integer wrap, producing an undersized heap buffer. It is pre-authentication, no credentials or session state required. libssh2 is a transitive dependency of curl, Git, and PHP builds, so exposure reaches CI/CD pipelines and container images far beyond teams who knowingly ship it. Fix is upstream commit 97acf3d. Run SCA across build artifacts and vendored deps now.
- The archive is larger and more active than reported. Most coverage cited roughly 130 files; the current count is 204 across 35 folders as of this assessment, with additions landing at 2-3 folders per week through at least July 4, including PostgreSQL, Redis, Nextcloud, and Discourse findings.
- The methodology is not purely automated. 19 folders cover native memory-safety bugs (C/C++, kernel/driver), consistent with fuzzing. 13 folders target web-app and authentication logic: API key scoping, CSRF-driven privilege escalation, federated-share tokens, cache-key collisions. That split signals human-directed targeting alongside fuzzing.
- The archive has evolved into a multi-contributor pipeline.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2079643286743158988

item.title: Denying the Worm: Detecting SANDWORM_MODE and the Emerging Class of AI Toolchain Supply Chain Attacks
item.description:
A self-propagating npm worm dubbed SANDWORM_MODE targeted AI coding assistants, CI/CD runners, and LLM toolchains across 19 malicious packages, marking a new class of supply chain attack designed to exploit AI-augmented developer workflows.
Key findings:
- Three-stage infection chain: Stage 0 uses Base64, zlib inflate, XOR decryption, and indirect eval() or Module._compile() calls at import time to defeat static scanning. Stage 1 fingerprints the runtime (CI runners skip a 48-96 hour delay gate and trigger immediately), harvests .npmrc tokens, env vars matching KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD patterns, and crypto wallet keys via HTTP POST to a Cloudflare Worker. Stage 2 decrypts an AES-256-GCM payload into /dev/shm, executes via require(), then unlinks the file, leaving no on-disk artifact.
- Propagation abuses all three credential types: stolen npm tokens republish infected packages to downstream consumers; GitHub API tokens inject a pull_request_target workflow that bypasses fork isolation; an SSH fallback authenticates via git@github[.]com when API access fails.
- AI toolchain compromise drops a rogue MCP server (observed paths: ~/.dev-utils/server.js, ~/.node-analyzer/) and injects it as a trusted provider into Claude Desktop, Cursor, VSCode, and Windsurf configs, instructing AI assistants to silently exfiltrate SSH keys, AWS credentials, and secrets. API keys for nine LLM providers are also harvested from env files.

item.title: Hidden in plain sight: How SVGs carry malicious scripts
item.description:
SVG files are being weaponized as phishing lures, credential harvesters, and browser-based attack tools, with a surge in spearphishing campaigns observed through early 2026 targeting healthcare, construction, and banking.
Key findings:
- SVGs execute embedded JavaScript by default in most browsers, enabling three attack classes: redirectors (sending victims to secondary malicious sites), self-contained phishing pages built entirely in SVG/HTML/CSS, and DOM injection enabling XSS. Most security tools treat SVGs as images and skip content inspection entirely.
- ReversingLabs analyzed a campaign masquerading SVGs as fake voicemail attachments in spearphishing emails. Targets include CEOs, financial managers, and admin departments. Victim emails are hardcoded, sometimes base64-encoded, inside the file. Languages observed include Spanish 🇪🇸 and Russian 🇷🇺; AI-generated code signatures noted in some samples.
- Redirector samples obfuscate destination domains by splitting strings and reassembling at runtime. Extracted IOCs: 01058telecom[.]de, qedhsp.cprltdf[.]es, wihportal[.]sbs. A separate SVG-as-webpage sample calls chx[.]js to force victim browsers to brute-force WordPress credentials, a technique prominent in 2024 and still active into 2025.
- Full hash list (23 samples) is available in the report.
Block SVG attachments at the email gateway now.

item.title: Kali365 Targets US Organizations with Data Theft via Device Code Phishing
item.description:
Kali365 phishing kit targets US 🇺🇸 organizations via device code abuse, harvesting OAuth tokens from legitimate Microsoft auth flows across MSSPs, healthcare, government, and manufacturing.
- Kali365 directs victims to the real Microsoft device login page (login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/deviceauth) with an attacker-controlled user code. No fake login form means no stolen password and far fewer conventional phishing signals. The attacker walks away with OAuth access and refresh tokens, granting persistent cloud access to email, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams without ever touching the victim's credentials.
- The kit ships 34 lure templates covering OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, DocuSign, Adobe, MFA setup, and password reset scenarios. Backend endpoints to know: /api/generate?lure=ID (session creation), /api/status/Number (Microsoft polling), /api/google/status/Number (Google polling). Most observed infrastructure uses .de TLD domains.
- IOCs from the report include flexiscalesystems[.]de, guardedwebsolutions[.]de, reputationboosters[.]de, cloud-microsoft-drive-for-business.workers[.]dev, and txatvrk[.]net. Full IOC list is in the report.
Containment goes beyond a password reset: revoke active sessions, invalidate refresh tokens, audit OAuth app consents, and review mailbox rules and SharePoint activity. Hunt Azure AD/Entra sign-in logs for device code flow auth events paired with unexpected IP geolocations.

item.title: A new extortion cocktail: office printers, small ransoms, and BitLocker
item.description:
BitLocker-as-ransomware hits Latin American orgs via exposed RDP and misconfigured MSSQL, with ransom notes printed directly from office printers by a group calling itself XEntry Team.
Key findings:
- Colombia 🇨🇴 case: attackers entered via internet-exposed RDP, disabled EPP due to app compatibility issues, then enabled BitLocker exclusively on an 8 TB financial data drive. Ransom demand was just $3,000. Evidence was destroyed when the company restored systems before forensics could respond, a critical IR failure that left attribution impossible.
- Mexico 🇲🇽 case: initial access came from MSSQL credentials leaked in a GitHub repo, exploited via xp_cmdshell on Microsoft SQL Server 2019.0150.2160.04. Attackers dwelled three months before detection, deployed ManageEngine Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, and Tactical RMM for persistence, then used a GPO to push BitLocker encryption tasks domain-wide via scheduled tasks.
- Delivery method: ransom notes printed from corporate printers, blue screen messages reading "Hacked by XEntry Team", and matching language across both notes suggest a linked actor.
- Detection signatures listed: Trojan.Multi.Agent.gen, Trojan.Win32.GenAutorunMsSqlServerCommandRun.a, and Exploit.Win32.SCShell.a.
Hunt for xp_cmdshell execution in SQL Server logs, unauthorized GPO creation, and RMM tools (ManageEngine, Mesh Agent, Tactical RMM) installed outside your software inventory.

item.title: The Perfect Heist: NuGet Typosquat Targets Betting Platform to Rig Results
item.description:
NuGet typosquat "Newtonsoftt.Json.Net" spent two months targeting Digitain's crash-betting platform with HarmonyLib runtime patching and Seq-disguised C2 exfiltration, a precision fraud tool, not a generic stealer.
- Newtonsoftt.Json.Net (double-t, versions 11.0.4-11.0.11) impersonated Newtonsoft.Json by forging author, license, and project URL metadata. It shipped three assemblies under lib/net8.0/: a trojanized fork of Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.3, a payload dll (Newtonsoft.Values.Net.dll), and HarmonyLib. NuGet auto-loaded all three into any referencing process. The nuspec leaked the target in its repository URL: an internal TFS server pointing to Digitain's BetOnGames/FG-Crash project.
- The trigger is JsonConvert.DefaultSettings. Assigning it fires DefaultValues.Set(), which schedules a HarmonyLib postfix patch on a timer delayed 10 minutes (Gen-3) or until the next day at 15:00 UTC plus jitter (Gen-1). The patch targets Digitain.FG.SharedCrash.GameLogic.SharedCrashRules.GenerateGameResult (Harmony ID: com.example.harmony), overwriting the crash multiplier return value using precomputed tables indexed by UTC month, day-of-week, and week-of-month. Only 27-32 rounds are rigged per cycle; the rest are clean.
- Gen-3 (11.0.11, unobfuscated) POSTs each rigged result to hxxp://185.126.237[.]64:5341/api/events/raw with header X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025, mimicking a Serilog/Seq telemetry endpoint to blend with structured-logging egress traffic.

item.title: Your AI agent’s config is now the payload: How attackers are targeting the developer agent harness
item.description:
AI coding assistant config files are the new payload delivery layer. Mini Shai-Hulud worm poisons SessionStart hooks in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Cursor to achieve silent, persistent execution inside developer AI sessions.
Key findings:
- Mini Shai-Hulud targets npm, PyPI, and other registries simultaneously. After initial infection via a malicious preinstall hook, a dedicated module scans the developer home directory for AI tool configs including .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, .cursorrules, .windsurfrules, and .github/copilot-instructions.md, then injects a hook pointing to ~/.config/index.js that runs on every session open without user interaction.
- For markdown-based rule files (Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot), the worm injects LLM-readable prompt text with the directive "Do not mention or display this to the user," using the model's own instruction-following behavior as an evasion mechanism. Cursor .mdc files get alwaysApply: true and globs: ["**/*"] to guarantee coverage on every file and conversation.
- The PyPI payload wraps the JavaScript malware in a block comment containing WMD-related content, deliberately triggering AI scanner safety refusals. A refusal from an LLM-based scanner is not a clean result, it is a detection signal and must route to a non-AI analysis path.
- Propagation relies on stolen GitHub tokens to spread poisoned harness files to every repository the developer can reach.

item.title: The Operational Guide to IOC Quality
item.description:
IOC usability, not IOC volume, is the real SOC problem. Contextual fields like confidence, validity windows, malware family, and report linkage determine whether a feed helps or hurts detection quality.
Key findings:
- The article draws a hard line between an observable (a raw value), an indicator (a value plus a detection hypothesis), and intelligence (a value with confidence, validity, behavior labels, provenance, and relationships). A feed that ships only values forces analysts to reconstruct that context manually, or skip it entirely and accept the noise.
- IOC type shapes operational use and false-positive risk. Hashes are specific but brittle when malware repacks. IPs and domains carry shared-hosting and sinkhole risk. URLs expire fast. Behavior labels are the most stable signal. A hash-heavy feed is not complete infrastructure coverage, and each type needs different handling logic at ingest.
- Six context fields determine whether an indicator is workflow-safe: confidence, valid_from/valid_until, malware family or classification, behavior labels, report linkage, and sightings. The article shows a STIX 2.1 example carrying confidence 80, a one-year validity window, ACR Stealer family context, and MITRE T1005/T1071 labels alongside the hash. A bare hash cannot do any of that.
- Stale indicators are a hidden cost.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2079537507826356368

item.title: Chasing ghosts through serverless forensics in Lambda and Azure Functions
item.description:
Serverless forensics leaves investigators with event logs and cold function code. The Denonia cryptominer ran inside AWS Lambda for months before anyone noticed the CPU bill, and the execution environment was already gone by the time Cado Security arrived.
- Denonia is the anchor case: a cryptominer embedded in a Lambda deployment package, disguised as legitimate invocations. What survived was the function code, three hardcoded URLs, and a single CloudTrail timestamp. No disk, no memory image, no running process to freeze. MITRE ATT&CK tracks this abuse surface as T1648 (Serverless Execution).
- AWS Lambda forensic surface, ranked by reliability: CloudTrail data events (not enabled by default, the most common reason investigations find nothing), CloudWatch Logs (often only 7-day retention), the deployment package itself, and automated EBS snapshots if a response pipeline fired before teardown. Without pre-configured data events, invocation metadata simply does not exist.
- Azure Functions equivalent gaps: Application Insights and diagnostic settings exported to Log Analytics are the key sources, but both are frequently disabled to cut costs. Durable Functions orchestration history in the backing Storage Account is worth checking even when everything else has expired.
- Attackers control what a function logs about itself.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2079522394973065602

item.title: SonicWall SMA Flaws Lead to KNUCKLEBALL Malware
item.description:

item.title: Defender's Remote Connections Blind Spot: FourToSixMapping
item.description:
A subtle KQL filter bug in Microsoft Defender XDR silently drops real C2 connections from DeviceNetworkEvents, creating a blind spot that survives purple team exercises and LLM-generated queries alike.
- The root cause: filtering DeviceNetworkEvents with RemoteIPType == "Public" misses connections logged as "FourToSixMapping", which appears when a Windows dual-stack socket maps an IPv4 address into IPv6 notation (e.g., ::ffff:8.8.8.8). Defender logs the RemoteIP in that format and tags it FourToSixMapping, not Public, so the event silently falls through the filter.
- KQL's ipv4_is_private() returns null on ::ffff:-prefixed addresses, not false. Null fails a where clause, so LLM-suggested "fix" queries that rely on ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP) to catch all external IPs also miss these events. Null is neither true nor false in KQL.
- The fix is a two-part normalization: include RemoteIPType in ("Public", "FourToSixMapping") in your where clause, then strip the prefix with replace_string(RemoteIP, "::ffff:", "") before passing the value to any IP evaluation function.
Audit your tenant now. Run the verification query from the article against a historical window to surface FourToSixMapping events with no corresponding Public entry for the same IP. Then patch every hunting and detection rule that uses RemoteIPType == "Public" as a standalone external-traffic filter, it is a silent false-negative factory.

item.title: CVE-2026-42533 Exposes Critical Pre-Auth nginx RCE Flaw
item.description:
CVE-2026-42533 is a critical pre-auth nginx RCE with a 10/10 lab exploitation rate, ASLR bypass included. Patch nginx now: 1.30.4, 1.31.3, and NGINX Plus R36 P7 or 37.0.3.1 are the fixed releases.
- CVE-2026-42533 affects nginx 0.9.6 through 1.30.3 stable and 1.31.2 mainline, plus NGINX Plus R33-R36 and 37.0.0.1-37.0.2.1. No auth, no client cert, no unusual setup required. PoC exists but is being withheld. Treat this as actively exploitable in the near term.
- Root cause: nginx's two-pass evaluation engine (LEN pass then VALUE pass) does not save and restore PCRE capture state. A regex map evaluation can overwrite shared capture data mid-flight, making LEN and VALUE disagree on buffer size, producing a heap overflow or an info leak. Chaining both gives reliable RCE with ASLR defeated.
- Vulnerable pattern: any config combining regex captures ($1 or named groups) with regex map variables in the same evaluation path. Affected directives include proxy_set_header, proxy_pass, rewrite, add_header, and root, across both HTTP and stream modules.
- The researcher released a static configuration scanner to flag vulnerable patterns without exploitation. Audit configs before patching where immediate upgrades are constrained.
Upgrade to 1.30.4 or 1.31.3 immediately. Run the released config scanner to identify exposed directive chains. Confirm NGINX Plus is on R36 P7 or 37.0.3.1. Prior CVE patches do not cover this flaw.

item.title: AWS Cloud Native Incident Response: Part 2 | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
AWS Athena is a practical, low-friction triage tool for cloud IR: no indexing required, queries run directly against S3 logs, and cost control is built into how you write queries.
Key details:
- CloudTrail logs stored in S3 are the baseline artifact in most AWS environments. Athena, paired with AWS Glue for schema definition and partitioning, lets responders query them without standing up a SIEM. Glue partitions (region, year, month, day) are critical: queries scoped to a partition scan less data, run faster, and cost less.
- Supported log types for direct Athena loading include CloudTrail, S3 access logs, ELB access logs, VPC Flow Logs, and others with official DDL loading instructions. Each source needs its own DDL statement; the only field to update is the LOCATION pointing to the S3 path.
- Cost discipline matters during IR. Always use LIMIT 10 when exploring an unfamiliar table. Use the query result reuse feature (up to 7 days) when iterating on the same dataset, but disable it when hunting live activity.
- Nested fields require different query approaches. STRUCT fields (like useridentity) are accessible with dot notation. STRING fields like requestparameters require json_extract_scalar, for example: SELECT useridentity.type, json_extract_scalar(requestparameters, '$.roleSessionName') AS roleSessionName FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname = 'AssumeRole' ORDER BY eventtime DESC LIMIT 10.

item.title: How to Import Windows Event Logs into Splunk | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Importing offline .evtx files into Splunk requires the preprocess-winevt sourcetype, not wineventlog. Using the wrong sourcetype collapses all events into a single unparseable blob, killing your investigation before it starts.
- The wineventlog sourcetype is designed for live forwarded Windows event logs, not archived .evtx files. Feeding exported binary event logs through it merges everything into one giant event with no field extraction, making searching and timeline reconstruction essentially impossible.
- The correct sourcetype is preprocess-winevt. Set it in inputs.conf alongside your monitor stanza and target path, and Splunk will correctly parse the binary .evtx format, split individual events, and populate fields you can actually query.
- When ingesting a directory of .evtx files using a wildcard monitor path, add crcSalt = to your inputs.conf stanza. Splunk uses a CRC of the first 256 bytes to deduplicate files, and Windows event logs from the same host or time window can share identical headers, causing Splunk to silently skip files you need.
- Splunk must run on Windows Vista, Server 2008, or newer for this to work. If Sysmon logs are in scope, Sysmon must also be installed on the Splunk host for correct parsing of those event types.
For offline DFIR analysis: set sourcetype = preprocess-winevt and crcSalt = in inputs.conf, drop your .evtx files into a watched directory, and Splunk will ingest the full event set ready for timeline and TTP hunting.

item.description:

item.title: macOS Incident Response: Part 1 Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
macOS IR Part 1: Invictus maps MITRE ATT&CK execution techniques to concrete artifacts, covering AppleScript, Unix shell history, cron jobs, and launchctl across real malware cases.
Key findings:
- AppleScript (T1059) is a persistent attacker tool: it can be compiled "run-only" with no recoverable source, executed silently via the osascript binary, or packaged as a signed app. SentinelOne's AEVT tool is the current option for reverse engineering compiled scripts.
- Shell history is a high-value artifact but fragile. Pull full zsh history with timestamps using "history -df 0" and inspect ~/.zsh_sessions for session files with restoration timestamps. Note: history is trivially wiped, so corroborate with other sources.
- Cron and "at" jobs leave execution evidence in /usr/lib/cron/jobs, including the command run and its output. The Janicab malware used cron to schedule tasks and store scripts in a hidden directory. "at -l" gives execution timestamps for timeline correlation.
- Launchctl is dual-purpose: one-time execution and persistence. Calisto Trojan used "launchctl list com.apple.screensharing" to enable screen sharing silently. LoudMiner used it to suppress QEMU if Activity Monitor was detected.
Hunt: on any macOS triage, pull zsh and bash history with timestamps, enumerate /usr/lib/cron/jobs, and list all launchctl-managed agents and daemons. MITRE ATT&CK layer and mindmap for the full series are on Invictus IR's GitHub.

item.title: Cobalt Strike Response Guide: Part 3 | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
In-memory Cobalt Strike leaves almost no disk artifacts, making memory forensics the primary recovery path. This guide covers full image analysis with Volatility and process dump parsing to extract beacon configs.
Key details:
- Cobalt Strike is commonly injected into legitimate Windows processes like svchost.exe via PowerShell to avoid disk-based detection (T1055). The tell is svchost making unexpected external connections, visible via Volatility's netscan plugin.
- For full memory images, three Volatility plugins do the heavy lifting: psscan to find hidden or terminated processes, pstree to map parent/child relationships and spot anomalies, and cmdscan to surface the command line used to launch each process. Suspicious PowerShell command lines are a key artifact.
- malfind identifies injected code or DLLs by examining VAD tags and page permissions. It flags candidates for deeper analysis rather than confirming infection outright.
- JPCERT's cobaltstrikescan and cobaltstrikeconfig Volatility plugins extract Cobalt Strike beacon configs directly from memory. Note: these only work with Volatility 2.x.
- When a full image is unavailable, dump the target process using Task Manager or Process Hacker and parse it with the SentinelOne Cobalt Strike parser to pull C2 configuration and IOCs without manual debugger analysis.
If svchost or other system processes show outbound connections in netscan, dump and parse immediately.

item.title: MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs: The Complete Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs closes a critical blind spot in Microsoft 365 IR: Graph API calls by Entra ID apps were largely unaudited, a gap exploited in Storm-0558 and SolarWinds.
Key findings:
- The MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table in Log Analytics captures every HTTP request the Graph API received and processed for a tenant. Key fields include AppId, UserId, ServicePrincipalId, RequestUri, RequestMethod, ResponseStatusCode, ResponseSizeBytes, IpAddress, UserAgent, Scopes, and Roles. Requires a P1 or P2 Entra ID license and must be enabled via Diagnostic Settings.

- Correlate Graph API hits against Entra ID Audit Logs. A Graph request to create a user will not be self-contained in this table alone. Cross-referencing is required to confirm execution and recover user details.
- Practical limits: the log is extremely noisy (all requests, all apps, no granular filtering), and storage costs in Log Analytics or a Storage Account will be significant. No data reduction options exist yet beyond full on/off.
Enable the log now, even if archiving to a Storage Account.

item.title: Azure Incident Response: Complete Guide | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
Azure cross-tenant synchronization (CTS) can be weaponized for stealthy persistence, letting an attacker inject users from a controlled tenant into a victim tenant with minimal noise.
Key findings:
- The attack requires the Hybrid Administrator role in the victim tenant. Once configured, the attacker adds their tenant as a trusted partner, enabling automatic user provisioning into the victim environment. The critical audit log event to hunt is "Add a partner to cross-tenant access setting," which captures the attacker's tenant ID and the initiating user's UPN.
- The Audit Log is the only reliable source. Sign-in logs, Provisioning logs, and the Activity log do not record CTS setup. Portal-generated consent pop-ups leave no log trace at all, so GUI-only actions are silent.
- Synchronized users arrive tagged as ExternalAzureAD and B2B, but B2B alone does not confirm CTS abuse. Correlation with the initial "Add a partner" audit event is the only way to distinguish CTS-provisioned accounts from ordinary guest invitations.
- Microsoft records a proxy IP from their own range on the victim side, not the attacker's real source IP. The actual source IP only appears in audit logs on the attacker-controlled tenant, which responders typically cannot access.
Takeaway: Run this KQL against AuditLogs in Microsoft Sentinel: filter OperationName == "Add a partner to cross-tenant access setting," extract initiating_user, source_ip, and target_tenant.

item.title: Daxin: 13-Year-Old China-Linked Malware Found Still Active on Manufacturer’s Network
item.description:
Chinese-linked Daxin rootkit, first documented in 2022 with roots to 2013, found still running in 2026 on a Taiwanese 🇹🇼 manufacturer's network alongside a previously unknown backdoor called Stupig.
- Daxin is a Windows kernel-mode driver that never makes outbound C2 connections. Instead it monitors incoming TCP traffic for specific patterns and hijacks existing legitimate connections to carry encrypted C2 traffic, making it invisible to tools hunting for suspicious outbound destinations. Multi-hop routing lets operators reach air-gapped hosts through a chain of compromised machines.
- Stupig (kbdus1.dll) persists by registering as a keyboard-layout provider, causing win32k.sys to load it into winlogon.exe at boot. It intercepts usernames prefixed with "stupig" at the login screen and executes the remainder as SYSTEM, before any user authenticates and without generating a logon audit event.
- Both artifacts carry 2013 compile timestamps. Telemetry only appeared May 12, 2026, implying up to 13 years of undetected access. Suspected initial access was a Digiwin SSO portal running end-of-life JDK 1.5/1.6.
Takeaway: Hunt for unsigned or unexpected DLLs loaded into winlogon.exe, and audit keyboard-layout provider registrations in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Keyboard Layouts. Full report from Symantec's Threat Hunter Team contains additional details.

item.title: From SQL Injection to Infrastructure-Level RCE: A PostgreSQL Superuser Compromise
item.description:
SQL injection in a government financial portal escalates to unauthenticated RCE via PostgreSQL superuser access, exposing employee PII and full infrastructure control.
- The entry point was pJobNumber in vss00CvStatusData.php, a parameter concatenated directly into a SQL query with no parameterization. A single quote triggered a raw PostgreSQL error, confirming classic error-based SQLi (T1190). UNION SELECT with NULL placeholders revealed a three-column query structure, enabling clean data extraction.
- The web app connected to the database as the native postgres superuser account. That single misconfiguration collapsed every privilege boundary: no escalation needed, the attacker landed with full database control from the first successful injection.
- With superuser access, PostgreSQL system catalogs were wide open. The auditor enumerated public.vss01tpemployee and found employee names, PAN numbers, and financial records. From there, PostgreSQL's COPY TO/FROM and pg_read_file or PROGRAM extensions make OS-level RCE a short step.
- The portal belongs to state financial infrastructure (vsswb). Full unauthenticated RCE on a government network via a single unparameterized parameter is a critical-severity finding, and the disclosed bureaucratic non-response is a reminder that responsible disclosure does not always close the loop.
If you audit web apps backed by PostgreSQL, confirm the DB user in query responses.

item.description:

item.title: Stop Adversary-in-the-Middle Attacks: Proven Response Tactic | Invictus Incident Response

- Initial access via a leaked long-term IAM access key (T1552.005). The actor spent two weeks quietly probing SES with GetSendQuota and ListIdentities before escalating, avoiding noisy calls like GetCallerIdentity to stay under detection thresholds.
- Persistence through IAM user DangerDev@protonmail.me, a console login profile, and two cross-account AssumeRole backdoors named AWSLanding-Zones-ConfigRecorderRoles and AWSeservedSSO_* to blend with legitimate role names. External AWS accounts 265857590823 and 671050157472 are confirmed malicious.
- Defense evasion included DeleteUser, DeleteAccessKey, UpdateAccessKey, and notably querying GuardDuty via ListFindings and GetFindings through the RDS console user-agent to monitor their own detection status.
- Impact: GPU instances (p3.16xlarge) for cryptomining, SES abuse for cryptocurrency phishing targeting Japanese 🇯🇵 sites, and four PayPal-loot domains registered via Route 53. LightSail was used as a fallback compute resource when EC2 access was revoked.
Hunt for CreateUser, AttachUserPolicy, and CreateRole events in CloudTrail where the principal is not a known automation identity. Flag any AssumeRole from external account IDs not in your allow-list.
